rationale: A wins because it knows where the story can actually stand up and where it collapses. Its best angle, "Mindbody Says AI Cut Fitness No-Shows by 22% — and It's Rolling Out to 50,000 Studios," puts the real proof burden right on the table instead of pretending the company metric is gospel. B has useful instincts, but "Mindbody's AI treats 50,000 studios' booking calendars as one data set" overclaims a shared dataset the update does not prove, and "Why a private Mindbody bundled its AI feature instead of charging extra for it" stretches a pricing footnote into a private-equity strategy story before the ownership facts exist.
gaps_in_A: "While Fitness Apps Race to Build AI Coaches" needs an external contrast case; A admits this, but the headline still leans on a market comparison not supplied in the update.
"Mindbody Owns the Studio Software, the Consumer Marketplace, and Now the AI That Fills Both" is strong but slightly overstates "fills both" before proving any operational ClassPass connection.
The "24hr" decay on the lead data angle may be too harsh; the 22% pilot claim could support a reported trade story beyond same-day launch if Mindbody supplies a named studio.
gaps_in_B: "Mindbody's AI treats 50,000 studios' booking calendars as one data set" invents a networked data premise. The update says Mindbody powers 50,000 studios and uses booking data, not that it pools all calendars into one dataset.

"Why a private Mindbody bundled its AI feature instead of charging extra for it" turns "privately held after a take-private deal" into "answering to private owners" and "PE-owned SaaS" without ownership facts in the update.

"The AI upgrade boutique fitness startups promised" depends on unnamed AI-native challengers and a promised upgrade B does not substantiate. It asks for a competitor in proof, but the angle is already leaning on the claim.
"adding AI to both" in the ClassPass angle is not grounded. The update says the assistant fills studio cancellations; nothing says ClassPass receives or uses the AI.
